opening_question: When a consciousness theory points to brain activity, behavior, or information flow, is it explaining consciousness itself or only explaining how we detect it?
core_claim: Kuhn's short section is a methodological warning for the whole taxonomy: theories of consciousness repeatedly slide between epistemology, meaning how consciousness can be known or measured, and ontology, meaning what consciousness really is. They also slide between correlation and causation: a neural, behavioral, or informational pattern may track consciousness without producing it, constituting it, or being sufficient for it. This is not a rival theory so much as a burden every theory must carry. A serious account has to say what evidence it accepts, what kind of thing it takes consciousness to be, and how it moves from observed regularities to causal or constitutive explanation.
strongest_case: The strongest case for giving these tensions their own section is that they expose the common failure mode of otherwise very different theories. Chalmers, Levine, Jackson, and Nagel press the epistemology-ontology problem from the first-person side: even complete functional or neural knowledge can seem to leave open what experience is like, whether Mary learning red, the explanatory gap, or the bat's alien point of view. The neuroscience of consciousness presses the same problem from the third-person side. The NCC program made consciousness empirically tractable by searching for minimal neural systems linked to specific experiences, but serious reviews now emphasize that mere correlates can be prerequisites, consequences, report demands, attention, memory, or hidden common causes rather than the basis of experience itself. Causal modeling, lesion work, stimulation, no-report paradigms, adversarial collaborations, and theory-driven predictions are attempts to tighten that inference. The evolutionary question adds another layer: some researchers model consciousness as a gradual, multidimensional biological profile across animals, while others look for transition markers such as unlimited associative learning or defend sharper thresholds. Panpsychist and fundamental-consciousness views push the ontological question furthest by denying that consciousness can simply emerge from nonconscious matter. Kuhn's framing is therefore strongest as an audit tool: before accepting any consciousness theory, ask what it knows, what it claims exists, and what kind of causal evidence would actually discriminate it from competitors.
best_objections: The main objection is that the frame is so general that it does not adjudicate much by itself. A physicalist, dualist, panpsychist, illusionist, global-workspace theorist, IIT theorist, and higher-order theorist can all agree that epistemology differs from ontology and that correlation differs from causation, then disagree completely about what follows. A second objection is that clean separation may be unrealistic: in consciousness science, ontological claims are often constrained by report, behavior, clinical dissociation, and theory-laden measurements, so 'what exists' and 'how we know' are entangled in practice. A third objection is that causal language can mislead: if a neural process is identical with, constitutes, realizes, or grounds an experience, it may not be a cause in the ordinary event-to-event sense. Empirically, no-report paradigms, stimulation, lesions, anesthesia, sleep, and animal studies improve inference but still face confounds about access, attention, task demands, neuroplasticity, background enabling conditions, and hidden common causes. Evolutionary claims are also underdetermined: single-cell homeostasis is not yet evidence of phenomenal consciousness, simple gradients can erase important qualitative differences, and proposed cutoffs such as unlimited associative learning remain contested. Fundamental or primordial consciousness views avoid brute emergence but inherit the combination problem and often lack independent empirical tests.
credibility: Overall epistemic status: active philosophical debate. The correlation-causation problem, common-cause reasoning, causal modeling, and the search for explanatory rather than merely statistical neural correlates are mainstream scientific methodology. The first-person/third-person gap, explanatory gap, Mary, zombies, and bat-style arguments are active philosophical debate rather than settled science. Gradual or multidimensional animal-consciousness models are scientifically serious but still uncertain at the boundaries. Specific transition-marker proposals such as unlimited associative learning are speculative extensions with active critique. Claims that consciousness is fundamental or ubiquitous, as in panpsychism, are speculative extensions within academic philosophy; versions tied to spiritual or cosmic consciousness can become religious/spiritual metaphysics, and versions with no testable commitments should be treated as fringe/weakly evidenced claims.
listener_hooks: Mary in the black-and-white room: if she knows every physical fact about color vision before seeing red, does the first red experience reveal a new fact or only a new ability?
Nagel's bat: a complete objective science of echolocation may still fail to tell us what the world is like from the bat's point of view.

The dashboard-light problem: if one brain area lights up whenever a subject is conscious, is it the engine of consciousness, an indicator, a downstream report system, or a shared effect of a hidden cause?
No-report experiments: can researchers study conscious experience while removing the need to press a button, speak, remember, or prepare an answer?

Animal consciousness as dimmer switch or threshold: is consciousness gradually profiled across mammals, birds, octopuses, insects, and simpler organisms, or does some biological innovation make the lights come on?
Panpsychism's trade: it avoids creating experience from wholly nonexperiential matter, but then has to explain how tiny bits of experience combine into a unified mind.

sources.title: Consciousness
sources.citation: Van Gulick, R. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; surveys concepts of consciousness, first-person and third-person data, explanatory questions, causal status, and metaphysical options.

sources.title: The Neuroscience of Consciousness
sources.citation: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; explains why NCCs are an early step and why consciousness science must separate explanatory correlates from mere correlates.

sources.title: The Hard Problem of Consciousness
sources.citation: Weisberg, J. Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy; frames the hard problem as involving ontology, scientific explanation, introspection, and first-person knowledge.

sources.title: Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness
sources.citation: Chalmers, D. J. (1995). Journal of Consciousness Studies, 2(3), 200-219; distinguishes functional explanation from the problem of phenomenal experience.

sources.title: Epiphenomenal Qualia
sources.citation: Jackson, F. (1982). The Philosophical Quarterly, 32(127), 127-136; introduces Mary's-room knowledge argument as a vivid epistemology-ontology pressure case.

sources.title: Materialism and Qualia: The Explanatory Gap
sources.citation: Levine, J. (1983). Pacific Philosophical Quarterly, 64, 354-361; gives the explanatory-gap formulation behind many later debates.

sources.title: What Is It Like to Be a Bat?
sources.citation: Nagel, T. (1974). The Philosophical Review, 83(4), 435-450; classic argument that objective accounts can miss subjective point of view.

sources.title: Reichenbach's Common Cause Principle
sources.citation: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; provides the philosophical background for the idea that correlations may reflect direct causation, reverse causation, or hidden common causes.

sources.title: Causal Models
sources.citation: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; surveys structural and probabilistic causal models, latent common causes, interventions, and causal discovery.

sources.title: Toward a Neurobiological Theory of Consciousness
sources.citation: Crick, F., & Koch, C. (1990). Seminars in the Neurosciences, 2, 263-275; foundational statement of the modern neural-correlates research program.

sources.title: Neural correlates of consciousness: progress and problems
sources.citation: Koch, C., Massimini, M., Boly, M., & Tononi, G. (2016). Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 17, 307-321; distinguishes full NCCs, content-specific NCCs, background conditions, and no-report strategies.

sources.title: Distilling the neural correlates of consciousness
sources.citation: Aru, J., Bachmann, T., Singer, W., & Melloni, L. (2012). Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews, 36, 737-746; argues that contrastive NCC studies can mix true NCCs with prerequisites and consequences.

sources.title: No-report paradigms: Extracting the true neural correlates of consciousness
sources.citation: Tsuchiya, N., Wilke, M., Frassle, S., & Lamme, V. A. F. (2015). Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 19(12), 757-770; proposes removing report-related confounds from NCC studies.

sources.title: Theories of consciousness
sources.citation: Seth, A. K., & Bayne, T. (2022). Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 23, 439-452; reviews major empirical theories and emphasizes the difficulty of distinguishing them experimentally.

sources.title: Hard Criteria for Empirical Theories of Consciousness
sources.citation: Doerig, A., Schurger, A., & Herzog, M. H. (2020/2021). Cognitive Neuroscience, 12(2), 41-62; proposes stricter empirical criteria for evaluating competing theories.

sources.title: Animal Consciousness
sources.citation: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; current overview of animal-consciousness evidence, methodological disagreement, continuity, and distribution questions.

sources.title: Dimensions of Animal Consciousness
sources.citation: Birch, J., Schnell, A. K., & Clayton, N. S. (2020). Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 24(10), 789-801; argues against a single scale of animal consciousness and for multidimensional profiles.

sources.title: The Transition to Minimal Consciousness through the Evolution of Associative Learning
sources.citation: Ginsburg, S., Jablonka, E., and colleagues (2016). Frontiers in Psychology; proposes unlimited associative learning as a marker for the transition to sentience.

sources.title: Assessing unlimited associative learning as a transition marker
sources.citation: Irvine, E. (2021). Biology & Philosophy, 36, 21; argues that UAL is productive but not yet a successful transition marker as defined.

sources.title: Panpsychism
sources.citation: Goff, P., Seager, W., and Allen-Hermanson, S. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; surveys panpsychism as the view that mentality is fundamental and ubiquitous, including the combination problem.
